claims.text: An MLIP trained on selectively sampled ab initio configurations from both solid and liquid states can be used within thermodynamic integration to calculate phase free energies and entropy contributions.
MLIP local-environment descriptors can encode anharmonic vibrations relevant to the free-energy landscape near melting.
MLIP local-environment descriptors can encode electron–vibration coupling relevant to the free-energy landscape near melting.
MLIP local-environment descriptors can encode configurational-entropy effects relevant to the free-energy landscape near melting.
Training on a carefully selected subset of ab initio data encompassing relevant fluctuations and anharmonic effects will permit high-fidelity prediction of energies and forces.
Combining the trained MLIP with thermodynamic integration should reproduce the free energies and associated entropy terms of both solid and liquid phases.
The MLIP workflow will avoid much of the computational overhead of full AIMD trajectories.
The workflow will retain key entropy and anharmonicity features in free-energy evaluations.
The resulting free energies and melting temperatures will be within roughly 10% of AIMD or TOR-TILD results.
The MLIP-based workflow will reduce computational cost by at least approximately one order of magnitude.
The cost reduction will make multicomponent systems more tractable.
Explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD workflows are accurate but computationally expensive for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Obtaining free-energy landscapes that include vibrational entropy and anharmonicity through current workflows requires extensive molecular-dynamics sampling.
The proposed approach is expected to be most effective for elemental and binary systems near their melting points.
Extension to multicomponent or extremely anharmonic systems may require more rigorous active learning and additional validation.
Systems with very strong electron–vibration coupling may be challenging when relevant MLIP training data are sparse.
The proposed performance gain has not yet been demonstrated for very complex multicomponent high-entropy systems.
